title: Characters, items and builds
thesis: In a roguelike the character is assembled during the run, and the most interesting builds come from what the player finds and combines rather than from what they pick on a menu: power that lives in items, mutations and upgrades makes each run a different game. The talks converge on a few levers that decide whether that assembly stays interesting: how choices are offered, how densely the pieces connect, how much brokenness you tolerate, and whether each trait, item and body part gives the player something legible to act on.

sections.heading: Where character power lives: items, experience and the shape of advancement
sections.brief: Open with the foundational argument that a roguelike character's power has traditionally lived in its equipment: Michael Brough's reading of Vance's Cugel and of Rogue, where the rogue becomes a wizard by collecting items and the game itself changes under the same rules, with the D&D lineage of Vancian spells and the scroll-reading rogue as historical background. Then set out Brogue as the strongest worked case: Brian Walker replaces skill points with enchant scrolls and drops experience points so avoidance and trickery become viable builds, and Eric Billingsley (Into Ruins), John Harris and the Brogue dancepad commentary converge on what that buys (build variety, fleeing without falling behind, improvised classes no line of code defines). Contrast use-based training and its 'victory dancing' exploit in early Crawl, Shattered Pixel Dungeon adding talents because level-ups were dull, Fire Emblem's random level-ups and Shiren's levelling equipment. Close with the edges: games where the character does not grow at all (HyperRogue, Drakefire Chasm, Thousand Hells' iconic heroes), god-level endgames the Adams brothers want, the player as mechanically distinct from monsters, and Gillian Smith's open questions about self-assessed skills and atrophying inventory. Guidance: decide early where advancement lives, because it determines which builds are viable and whether combat is mandatory.

sections.heading: Character creation and classes: the first build decision
sections.brief: Argue that in build-heavy roguelikes the creation screen is the game's first pitch: Ben McGraw (Dungeons of Dredmor, Master of Magic) and Jason Grinblat (Caves of Qud) converge on creation as a creative act that floods the player with possibilities, with Moria as the historical origin. Then cover structures that multiply starting variety while keeping balance tractable: DCSS's species/background split, Qud's True Kin versus mutant fork with castes that matter less than mutations, Rogue's Gate's starting party. Stage the central disagreement about classes: Brian Walker argues classes are a poor return on content because a dominant build gets looked up, David Brevik describes Diablo's anything-goes design becoming a soup and Diablo II guiding players with restricted paths, and Andrea Roberts' complexity meter in Roundguard shows that a class choice is also a choice of complexity the player must be told about; Advanced Rogue's paladin code is a cautionary oddity. Finish with generated stats: Wildermyth keeps random stat bonuses small to stop rerolling, Dungeonmans forbids rerolls outright, Pokemon IVs make small differences decisive under permadeath, and Angband and Alphaman cut stats that did nothing. Guidance: every creation choice should say something about how the game will play, and anything that invites rerolling should be small.

sections.heading: Bodies as builds: mutation, grafting and transformation
sections.brief: Make the case that changing the character's body is a distinctive roguelike way to build, and that visible transformation is unusually memorable: lead with Thomas Biskup's grafting in Ultimate ADOM (body parts as powers, with adaptation costs and size limits) and Wildermyth's wolf-head transformations that story events can always reference, then Julian Day on why transformation matters. Show the mutation lineage converging across games: Caves of Qud's seventy-plus mutations that can approximate almost any archetype, levelled or bought from three random offers, with defects as a deliberate resource; DCSS Demonspawn forcing adaptation; Alphaman's Gamma World mutations acting as classes; NetHack's corpse intrinsics; Sea of Rifts' crew mutating. Then parts-based bodies: Cogmind taking parts from enemies with rampant destruction forcing rebuilds, and Polybot-7 showing that removing choice over attachment changes the whole feel; Ultimate ADOM's soul swapping, Chogue's pawn promotion and the tardigrade game built around one animal ability. End with Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans, where the player selects from a generator's mutations, a radiation dial sets risk, and ownership arises without control. Guidance: pair every body change with a cost or constraint, keep it visible, and decide how much control the player has over which change arrives.

sections.heading: Traits, personality and identity: characters players can read
sections.brief: Start from Cat Manning's definition of a trait as a simple word that gestures at personality and hooks clearly into mechanics, and Brenda Romero's rule that no trait should leave the player stuck. Then show the convergent warnings about trait sprawl: Manning's Sims 3 analysis (perceptually distinct but mechanically overlapping traits, the 10,000 bowls of oatmeal, expansion traits as shallow showcases, Absent-Minded wrecking the core loop), Romero limiting each Empire of Sin trait to one or two effects, and Wildermyth's finding that players remember only two traits per hero. Present techniques for active traits: Manning's chaste-as-active-behaviour example and Crusader Kings III's stress system, orthogonal traits, Empire of Sin's trait categories, age-based malleability and off-screen trait changes, Heat Signature's run-filtering traits, and Wildermyth relationships and non-swappable gear as characterisation. Close with identity: Florence Smith Nicholls on gendered archetypes, Xalavier Nelson Jr. on the beliefs embedded in racial stat traits, Aaron Reed building persona from expressive choices, Alexandra Leonhart on playing against type and identity-driven levelling, and Nathan Savant on skill trees as the person a character can imagine becoming. Guidance: fewer, legible, active traits wired into the core loop, and scrutiny of what your trait and stat assignments say about people.

sections.heading: Shaping the upgrade decision: offers, drafts and sets
sections.brief: Argue that how a choice is offered matters as much as what is offered. Lead with Andrew Cedotal's 'drafting mullet' (chance limits which combos are available, the player controls investment) and his Goldilocks warning that neither fully constructed nor fully random upgrades sustain play, then Lisa Brown's case for a small number of meaningful reactive decisions and Pandamander's System 2 framing, with Brown's bounce off Rogue Legacy's tree as the counterweight. Bring in what makes a single choice good: Shawn Main on choices that recontextualise each other and change the run, Cole Wehrle's near-binary choices that create regret, Sersa Victory's mutually exclusive treasure rooms, now-versus-later priesthood and risky powers, and Rift Wizard's circles of power nudging purchases. Then the granularity question: Alexander King on singleton drafting's friction, the fixed complexity budget, and set-based decks (Card Hunter's item-sized card groups, thematic bundles, fewer pruning needs), with Dream Quest and Smallest Quest treating cards as inventory. Guidance: choose the size and frequency of decisions deliberately and make each one expensive to get wrong.

sections.heading: Synergy and comboness: why combinations feel like discoveries
sections.brief: Define the thing players chase: Andrew Cedotal's formal definition of a combo (a subset worth more than the best unconditional subset of the same size) and his finding that comboness rises with non-obviousness, set beside Ezra Szanton's point that drafting is only interesting when value depends on other cards and James Cartlidge's account of the 'is this going to work' thrill. Walk through how combos are built and signalled: Isaac's intuitable penny engine versus Gungeon's theme-signalled back-end combos (Alice Lai), Hades upgrades that remove a downside or amplify an upside, Szanton's ordering of synergy types from obvious to obscure, Courtney Liessen's multipliers on the conversion equation, Shawn Main's shared building blocks (Dicey Dungeons' dice), and Alex Byaly on correlated stats enabling planning. End with cases: Rift Wizard's spell market and fire-ghost engine, Noita's wand slots and Slay the Spire's Grand Finale anticipation. Guidance: build synergy through shared resources and categories rather than explicit 'if X then Y' text, and give players enough hints to suspect a combo before they confirm it.

sections.heading: Designing the build space: networks, silos and run-to-run variety
sections.brief: Treat the whole set of upgrades as a designed network. Lead with Ezra Szanton's synergy network model (cards as nodes, synergies as edges) and his three failure states: sparse networks where the challenge outscales linear synergies, siloed clusters that put blinders on drafting, and the healthy target of weak clusters with pivot points, plus overlapping categories and implicit anti-synergies as tools; his goal of improvisation, where even the best player cannot force one plan. Set against it Alice Lai's Hades approach of deliberately bounded system silos (and splitting cross-silo abilities) to keep the space legible, about nine hammer options per weapon, and her warning that too many upgrades blend builds into 'powerful sludge'; Gavin Verhey's Magic experience converges with Szanton (overly strong signposts and Bloomburrow's synergy made the tenth draft repetitive; build-around uncommons, modal cards and format-speed balance keep drafts fresh). Then variety at scale: Casey Yano funnelling players toward goal strategies, McGraw's 55-choose-7 Dredmor space, DCSS's hundreds of caster strategies and bhauth's argument that polynomial cost curves produce more viable builds than linear ones, Asura's random skill-tree subsets, Dustin Freeman's warning about kitchen-sink universes, Shawn Main's combination count, and Tim Keenan locking the piece type per run to trade within-run variety for distinct runs. Guidance: keep clusters weakly connected, bound what each system can do, and cap how much a single run can collect.

sections.heading: Broken on purpose: power fantasy, exploits and balance
sections.brief: Lead with the genre's distinctive permission: Against the Storm's team sought the one-in-twenty build that breaks the game, Courtney Liessen argues players should feel they are 'cheating' by using systems as intended (Monster Train's shrunken cloned giant, Reality Break's rewrite mechanic), Ben McGraw says broken things are fun and names the Disgaea effect, and Dylan Gedig notes spectacular and self-destructive builds are what streamers share. Then Brian Walker's principle of turning power up and balancing by situationality instead, and Dan DiIorio's that boring content goes unused at any power level, so effects beat numbers. Set the counter-position: balance still matters in single-player, because Tangledeep's too-hard and too-easy jobs both earned negative reviews (Andrew Aversa labels difficulty and gates hard jobs), Verhey contrasts PvE tolerance with PvP, and McGraw warns combinatorial balance is a long slog. Finish with specific breakages and fixes: Tangledeep's 'infinite Mirai' escape rotation and pets giving extra actions on a grid, and Casey Yano's tuning of starter cards and the vanilla/French-vanilla/weird ratio. Guidance: allow rare breakage that is earned and situational, but label and fix what breaks the core loop or makes a choice trivially right or wrong.

sections.heading: Item design: niches, consumables and tools that bite on the world
sections.brief: Argue that individual items earn their place by posing a question. Lead with Jasper Cole (Backpack Hero) on items with many different functions so every pickup is a trade-off, and no item strictly better than another, then Michael Brough's case that bump combat needs limited-use items as an out. Tom Francis's principle that tools should have constraints and freedoms tied to what the generator shuffles, illustrated by Heat Signature's three teleporters, gives the strongest design rule. Then consolidation and reinvention of consumables: Into Ruins merging potions and scrolls into orbs, Alphaman's ripening berries, Rift Wizard's rescue consumables, Word Processor's keyboard-shortcut powers. Close with risk on items: Advanced Rogue's cursed consumables and deadly miscellaneous magic versus NetHack's curses that lock slots but keep function, and NetHack's free stethoscope as an example of bending realism to keep an item useful. Guidance: give each item a niche and a constraint that interacts with the level, and make danger readable rather than arbitrary.

sections.heading: Inventory: limits, space and the meaning of objects
sections.brief: Begin with Max Sahin's argument that because generated maps deny players a sense of place, items become the vessels of memory and emotional anchors, with his everyday-object grounding. Then the convergent case for limits that force hard choices: Darren Grey's inventory limits against +2-replaces-+1 upgrades, Catacomb Kids' 'no hammerspace' rule, Tangledeep's locked hotbar ending skill hoarding, Into Ruins' one-way descent triggering passives, and The Banished Vault's permanent building placement. Spatial inventory as its own build layer: Backpack Hero's grid arrangement building on Dicey Dungeons' size-as-cost and Deus Ex, with adjacency buffs making power visible. Finish with inventory in multiplayer: Leif Bloomquist's two-hands rule pushing cooperation and natural roles, and Tyriq Plummer's setup-and-payoff team items and grouping abilities. Guidance: make carrying capacity a decision surface, not an annoyance, and let what players carry accumulate meaning.
